title: Dominic and the Letters
premise: Marguerite Kavanagh, drowning in debt and denial, hires quiet bookbinder Dominic Hale to pose as her boyfriend at the Kavanagh family reunion — a weekend that stretches into months as her café teeters and their pretend intimacy turns inconveniently real. When Marguerite discovers Dominic has been secretly corresponding with her estranged mother for years, letters she never knew existed, loyalty to family collides with the truth of what she feels. At the auction of her grandmother's house, Marguerite must choose between saving the café with money offered on the condition she walk away from Dominic, or losing everything to keep him. She chooses truth: they save neither the café nor the house in full, but together open a small bakery-bookshop where the letters finally come home.
about_author: Felix Thornbury is the pen name of a former pastry cook who spent a decade working pre-dawn shifts in Dublin and Portland before turning to fiction. He writes love stories about people who mistake competence for armor.

chapters.title: Three Missed Payments
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A bank letter arrives the same morning her oven dies; she ices a wedding cake with shaking hands and tells no one. Emotional beat: pride hardening into isolation as she calculates exactly how many weeks of solvency remain.

chapters.title: The Invitation
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her mother's sister summons the whole Kavanagh clan to Gran's estate for a reunion and auction, and every relative will ask about 'that nice young man' Marguerite invented two Christmases ago. Beat: panic dressed as irritation; she needs a boyfriend by Saturday.

chapters.title: The Man Who Mends Books
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. In his cramped bindery, Dominic repairs a first edition Marguerite brings in as collateral-adjacent sentimentality. He notices her flour-burned knuckles and her refusal to accept pity. Beat: cautious curiosity — he recognizes another person running on fumes.

chapters.title: Terms of Employment
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. Over day-old croissants, Marguerite offers Dominic payment in pastries and awkward honesty: one weekend, one lie, nothing real. He agrees with unsettling calm. Beat: a contract built on mutual loneliness, each certain they're the only one acting.

chapters.title: Arrival at Ashfield House
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The reunion begins: aunts cataloguing him, cousins testing him, Gran's empty chair at the head of the table. Dominic performs devotion better than expected because he isn't entirely performing. Beat: belonging arriving through a door marked 'fake.'

chapters.title: Dessert
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Pressed to bake for the family, she makes Gran's lost lemon tart recipe from memory while Dominic quietly holds the kitchen door against intruding relatives. Their hands touch over the whisk. Beat: the fake date stops being fake somewhere between the filling and the glaze.

chapters.title: The Locked Writing Desk
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Asked to appraise Gran's writing desk for the auction, Dominic finds it locked — and recognizes the handwriting on an old envelope inside as one he knows intimately. Beat: dread; he realizes whose daughter Marguerite is, and how much he already knows about her family that she doesn't.

chapters.title: Weekend Extension
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The reunion ends but the lie doesn't; her mother asks them both to stay through the auction preparations. Marguerite says yes before thinking. Beat: wanting disguised as obligation, the first crack in her heart-is-a-muscle doctrine.

chapters.title: Letters I Never Sent
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV flashback interwoven with present. Seven years ago, a grieving woman began bringing damaged letters to his shop for restoration — letters from Marguerite's mother to Gran, unsent, unread. Dominic became her confidant without ever learning the family name. Beat: the weight of accidental complicity.

chapters.title: Café Hours
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Back home, the bank gives her ten days. Dominic starts showing up at closing time, ostensibly to read, actually to help inventory. Beat: domesticity sneaking in — two people building a routine neither will admit is a relationship.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Aunt Vivienne, executor of Gran's estate, offers to cover the café's debts if Marguerite signs away her claim to the house and stops 'distracting herself with strangers.' Beat: loyalty weaponized; family presented as a debt collector.

chapters.title: What Dominic Knows
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Torn between protecting his long-time client (Marguerite's mother) and the woman falling for him, Dominic drafts three confessions and burns all three. Beat: loyalty vs. truth made literal — the theme arrives at his own door.

chapters.title: First Real Fight
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Marguerite discovers Dominic meeting secretly with her mother outside the bakery and assumes an affair or a con. The fight strips both of them raw. Beat: the fake relationship collapses precisely because it stopped being fake.

chapters.title: The Desk Opens
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Alone at Ashfield House, Marguerite forces the desk and finds decades of her mother's unsent letters to Gran — and among them, restoration receipts signed D. Hale, dated back seven years. Beat: betrayal reassembling itself into bewilderment.

chapters.title: Her Side of It
chapters.summary: Mother's POV (single chapter). Marguerite's mother explains the estrangement: Gran disowned her choice of husband, and she wrote letters she never dared send, restoring them like wounds. Dominic was the only person who knew all of it. Beat: grief revealed as the family's true inheritance.

chapters.title: Ten Days to Zero
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The bank deadline lands, the auction is tomorrow, and Dominic hasn't called since the fight. She bakes through the night, deciding what she can live without. Beat: rock bottom as clarity — the heart isn't containable after all.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Both POVs converging. Bidders circle Ashfield House; Aunt Vivienne's ultimatum stands; Dominic arrives mid-auction and publicly returns every restoration fee, declaring the letters belong to Marguerite. Beat: climax — truth offered at maximum cost, in front of everyone.

chapters.title: The Whole Heart
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She refuses Vivienne's money, loses the bid on the house, and chooses Dominic in front of the assembled Kavanaghs — then reads one of her mother's letters aloud, cracking the family open. Beat: choosing risk over rescue; loyalty finally aligned with truth.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The house sells to strangers; the café closes its doors. But the family fracture shifts — her mother comes to the shuttered bakery with a box of Gran's recipes. Beat: mourning what was lost while recognizing what was found.

chapters.title: Empty Storefront, Full Ledger
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Scouting cheap rents, she and Dominic find a narrow storefront with room for ovens in back and bookshelves in front. They sign the lease with borrowed money and no safety net. Beat: hope rebuilt honestly this time, on shared terms instead of a contract.

chapters.title: Grand Opening
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The bakery-bookshop opens: her tarts beside restored letters displayed under glass, her mother behind the counter, reluctant aunts in the doorway. Beat: belonging achieved not by blood or contract but by daily choice.

chapters.title: The First Letter Home
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, epilogue. On the new shop's first quiet evening, Marguerite writes a letter of her own — to Gran, sent at last — and slides it into the mail slot beside Dominic's hand on her shoulder. Beat: resolution; the heart, uncontained, finally at rest.
